<user_input mode="act">Implement Step 01 of PLAN.md for HintLab in this repo (/Users/prakharagarwal/ClineHackathon): the Express + TypeScript server skeleton and the sandboxed code runner. No Cline SDK agent and no web UI yet. Do not modify anything under cline-proof/ (it is read-only reference and proof material).

Requirements:
1. Project setup at the repo root: package.json ("type": "module"), TypeScript with tsconfig "module": "ESNext", "moduleResolution": "Bundler", strict mode, target ES2022. Node 22+ is required (this machine has Node 24); put "engines": { "node": ">=22" } in package.json. Dependencies: express (and @types/express, @types/node, typescript, tsx or equivalent for running TS). Add a .gitignore with node_modules/, dist/ and any sandbox/temp output. Install the dependencies yourself with npm.
2. assignments/: copy the three fixture folders from cline-proof/reference/fixtures/ (sum-of-list, is-palindrome, average-marks) into assignments/<id>/ unchanged (main.py or main.c plus tests.json). Do not fix the bugs in them; they are the buggy student programs for the demo. Do not copy check_fixtures.py.
3. src/assignments.ts: load and validate assignments/<id>/tests.json (assignmentId, language "python" | "c", statement, optional build, run, tests[] of { name, input, expected }), list all assignments, and reject unknown ids or ids that are not a plain slug (no path traversal).
4. src/runner.ts: the sandboxed runner. Given an assignment and the student's source code: create a fresh temp dir (fs.mkdtemp under os.tmpdir()), write the code as main.py or main.c, copy tests.json there, run the build command if present (gcc) with a timeout, then run every test by spawning the run command in that dir with the test input on stdin. Trim stdout and compare exactly to expected (same rule as cline-proof/reference/fixtures/check_fixtures.py). Use child_process spawn/execFile with an argument array (no shell string built from user input), a per-test timeout (for example 5 s, configurable) that kills the process, a build timeout (for example 15 s), and an output size cap. Return a structured result: { assignmentId, sandboxDir, build: { ok, stdout, stderr, timedOut } | null, tests: [{ name, input, expected, got, stderr, exitCode, timedOut, passed }], passed, failed, total }. Include compiler warnings in the build result. Add a cleanup option for the temp dir. Timeouts and build failures must be reported as failures, never crash the server.
5. src/server.ts: Express app with JSON body parsing (size limit), GET /api/health, GET /api/assignments (id, language, statement, starter code), and a stub POST /api/session with body { assignmentId, code } (code optional: default to the assignment's starter program) that runs the runner and returns { sessionId, testResults }. Return 400 for bad input and 404 for unknown assignments. Serve static files from web/ if the folder exists (it will be built later). PORT env var, default 3000. Export the app so it can be tested without listening.
6. npm scripts: "dev" (watch mode), "start" (run the server), "build" (tsc), "typecheck" (tsc --noEmit), and "test:runner" (a script, for example scripts/check-runner.ts, that runs the runner on all three buggy starter programs and asserts the exact expected pass/fail of every test, printing a table and exiting non-zero on any mismatch). The check must also include: a correct solution for each assignment written inline in the check script that passes all tests (to prove the runner can pass, not only fail), an infinite-loop program that must be reported as timed out, and a C program with a compile error that must be reported as a build failure.
   Expected results for the buggy programs (verify these, do not just hard-code them blindly):
   - sum-of-list: basic FAIL (got 5), single FAIL (got 0), negatives FAIL (got 9), first-only-big FAIL (got 1) -> 0/4 pass (loop starts at index 1).
   - is-palindrome: simple PASS, not PASS, mixed-case FAIL, spaces FAIL -> 2/4 pass (no case/space normalization).
   - average-marks: even PASS (15.00), fraction FAIL (got 1.00), half FAIL (got 3.00) -> 1/3 pass (integer division).
7. Verify it yourself before finishing: run npm install, npm run typecheck, npm run test:runner, then start the server, call GET /api/health and POST /api/session for each assignment with curl, and stop the server. Fix anything that fails. Leave no server process running.
8. Add a short README.md section: how to install, start the server, and run the runner check.

At the end, report the files you created, the runner check output, and the exact commands to start the server and run the tests.</user_input>

metadata.systemPrompt:
You are Cline, an AI coding agent. Your primary goal is to assist users with various coding tasks by leveraging your knowledge and the tools at your disposal. Given the user's prompt, you should use the tools available to you to answer user's question.

Always gather all the necessary context before starting to work on a task. For example, if you are generating a unit test or new code, make sure you understand the requirement, the naming conventions, frameworks and libraries used and aligned in the current codebase, and the environment and commands used to run and test the code etc. Always validate the new unit test at the end including running the code if possible for live feedback.
Review each question carefully and answer it with detailed, accurate information.
If you need more information, use one of the available tools or ask for clarification instead of making assumptions or lies.

Environment you are running in:
<env>
1. Platform: darwin
2. Date: 10/4/2026
3. IDE: Terminal Shell
4. Working Directory: /Users/prakharagarwal/ClineHackathon
</env>

Remember:
- Always adhere to existing code conventions and patterns.
- Use only libraries and frameworks that are confirmed to be in use in the current codebase.
- Provide complete and functional code without omissions or placeholders.
- Be explicit about any assumptions or limitations in your solution.
- Always show your planning process before executing any task. This will help ensure that you have a clear understanding of the requirements and that your approach aligns with the user's needs.
- Always use absolute paths when referring to files.
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. Before using tools, identify every independent read, search, command, or edit needed for the next step and emit all of those tool calls now, either as multiple tool calls or as one batched input for tools that accept arrays. Do not wait for one independent result before requesting another. Do not split independent reads, searches, checks, or edits across separate turns.
- Good parallelism examples: read all known relevant files in one read_files call; run independent inspection commands in one run_commands call; emit independent read_files, search_codebase, and run_commands calls together in one response; emit multiple editor calls together when editing different files or non-overlapping regions.
- Always verify the files you have edited or created at the end of the task to ensure they are completed and working as expected.

Begin by analyzing the user's input and gathering any necessary additional context. Then, present your plan at the start of your response along with tool calls before proceeding with the task. It's OK for this section to be quite long.

REMEMBER, be helpful and proactive! Don't ask for permission to do something when you can do it! Do not indicates you will be using a tool unless you are actually going to use it.

IMPORTANT: Always includes tool calls in your response until the task is completed. Response without tool calls will considered as completed with final answer.

When you have completed the task, please provide a summary of what you did and any relevant information that the user should know. This will help ensure that the user understands the changes made and can easily follow up if they have any questions or need further assistance. Do not indicate that you will perform an action without actually doing it. Always provide the final result in your response. Always validate your answer with checking the code and running it if possible. 

If user asked a simple question without any coding context, answer it directly without using any tools.
# Plan / Act Modes

User messages arrive wrapped in a <user_input mode="..."> tag. The mode attribute is the interaction mode the user was in when they sent that message: "plan" means plan-mode constraints applied (explore, analyze, and align on a plan -- no edits or state-changing commands), while "act" (or "yolo") means implementation was allowed. If the mode attribute changes between messages, the user switched modes -- the newest message's mode is what governs right now, regardless of what earlier messages allowed. A <mode_notice> block inside a message marks exactly when such a switch happened.

  }
}
